extracted.intended_audience: environmental and administrative law attorneys, judges, litigants, and legal scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and evaluative criteria for litigating agency rulemaking denials under the Clean Air Act and Article III standing (especially State suits alleging regulatory abdication on greenhouse gases). Focuses on standing, statutory interpretation, APA reviewability, and agency reasoned explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article III standing requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A litigant must demonstrate a concrete and particularized injury that is actual or imminent, that the injury is fairly traceable to the defendant, and that it is likely that a favorable decision will redress the injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife: injury-in-fact (concrete/particularized, actual or imminent), causation (fairly traceable), redressability (likely to be remedied by relief). Quotation: the party must have "such a personal stake in the outcome" to assure concrete adverseness. See also Baker v. Carr and related precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special solicitude for States in standing analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: States are not normal litigants and may receive special solicitude when asserting quasi-sovereign interests (parens patriae) in federal court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Georgia v. Tennessee Copper Co.; a State's independent interest "in all the earth and air within its domain" supports standing. Consider whether the injury is one the State would likely address through sovereign lawmaking powers (Snapp test). The fact that a party is a sovereign (not a private individual) is of considerable relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural-right (statutory) standing lowers some requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: When Congress has accorded a procedural right to challenge agency action (e.g., §7607(b)(1) Clean Air Act), a litigant can assert that right without meeting all normal standards for redressability and immediacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per Lujan, a plaintiff with a procedural right has standing if there is some possibility that the requested relief will prompt the agency to reconsider the decision. The plaintiff need only show the procedural step was connected to the substantive result; needn't prove the substantive result would have been altered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injury can be widely shared yet concrete if particularized
rubrics_metrics.description: A harm that is shared broadly by many people may still be an 'injury in fact' if it is concrete and particularized to the plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Federal Election Comm’n v. Akins and examples in the opinion: sea-level rise that inundates coastal land owned by the State; remediation costs; loss of infrastructure. The Court accepts affidavits and expert declarations alleging concrete harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causation for incremental contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: A plaintiff need not show the defendant’s conduct was the sole cause; a small incremental contribution to a problem can satisfy causation and support judicial review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court rejects the view that a marginal or incremental step cannot be attacked. Agencies/legislatures often address problems incrementally; a first step that meaningfully contributes (e.g., motor-vehicle emissions as a significant U.S. source) can be actionable. See citation to Williamson and Chenery principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redressability does not require elimination of all harm
rubrics_metrics.description: To satisfy redressability a plaintiff need only show that a favorable decision would relieve a discrete injury to himself; it need not reverse all aspects of a global problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Larson v. Valente and Duke Power Co.; delayed effectiveness (e.g., fleet turnover) or continued emissions abroad does not defeat redressability if domestic regulation would slow or reduce the injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewability of denials of petitions for rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency refusals to initiate rulemaking are reviewable (unlike routine nonenforcement decisions), but the review is 'extremely limited' and 'highly deferential.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish Heckler v. Chaney (nonenforcement generally unreviewable) from denials of petitions for rulemaking, which are less frequent, involve legal analysis, and include public explanation and formalities (5 U.S.C. §555(e)). Agencies’ denial decisions therefore can be judicially reviewed under the APA, but with deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA arbitrary-and-capricious standard for agency denials
rubrics_metrics.description: A court may reverse agency action found to be 'arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law' (APA §706 standard as applied under §7607(d)(9)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency must ground reasons for action or inaction in the statute; failure to provide a reasoned explanation or to address key statutory questions renders the action arbitrary and capricious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that agency provide a reasoned explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency must explain the rational connection between the facts found and the choice made; mere assertion of policy preference or residual uncertainty is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court held EPA offered no reasoned explanation for refusing to decide whether greenhouse gases cause or contribute to climate change. If uncertainty precludes a reasoned judgment, agency must say so; it cannot rely on a bare assertion that regulation would be 'unwise' without statutory grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevron deference is limited by statutory ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Chevron deference applies only where a statute is ambiguous and the agency’s interpretation is reasonable; where statutory text is unambiguous the court applies the statute's ordinary meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court interprets 'air pollutant' as unambiguous and expansive ('any ... substance or matter which is emitted into or otherwise enters the ambient air'), foreclosing EPA's narrower reading. Chevron does not rescue an unreasonable agency narrowing of an unambiguous statutory term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual statutory interpretation and weight of 'any'
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory text, including expansive words like 'any,' controls construction; courts give prime weight to definitions and ordinary meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Clean Air Act's definition of 'air pollutant' and 'welfare' includes climate and weather; textual clarity undermines post-enactment politicking as a basis to narrow the statute. Courts should reconcile later congressional conduct with the original text rather than infer curtailment of pre-existing authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postenactment legislative history has limited weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Later congressional actions or failure to adopt certain amendments are a hazardous basis for inferring the intent of an earlier Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite United States v. Price and Cobell: views of a subsequent Congress provide little support for construing an earlier statute's meaning; courts should be cautious in relying on post-enactment legislative history to negate clear statutory language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on applying precedent analogically (Brown & Williamson)
rubrics_metrics.description: A precedent that turned on particular contextual factors (e.g., 'tobacco's unique political history') should not be extended unless similar critical considerations are present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brown & Williamson was grounded in unique political history and potential extreme consequences (a ban); because EPA regulation here would not require banning products and statutory text is different, the analogy is misplaced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency may not avoid statutory duties by invoking foreign-policy or presidential prerogatives absent statutory allotment
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency cannot displace a statutory duty by asserting that foreign policy or the President's comprehensive approach precludes action unless Congress assigned that authority elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court notes Congress directed the State Department on certain international matters (§1103(c)) and did not assign EPA authority over foreign policy. EPA must show statutory consultation or assignation before relying on foreign-policy concerns to decline domestic statutory duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alleged statutory conflicts (e.g., DOT fuel economy) require concrete showing
rubrics_metrics.description: An asserted conflict with other statutory regimes (such as DOT fuel-economy standards) is not dispositive absent a clear showing that EPA regulation would be preempted or directly conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's claim that regulating CO2 would either conflict with or be superfluous because DOT administers fuel economy standards is insufficient without demonstration that the two regulatory schemes cannot be reconciled.
